findings.issue_text: P1 confidence=100 packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/slots.ts:114 — `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` is always false because it compares distinct Dayjs objects by identity, so a zero-length date override is treated as an available interval instead of its closure semantics.

P1 confidence=100 packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/slots.ts:106 — `dateOverrides.find((date) => { ... if (slotEndTime.isBefore(...date.start...) || ... || slotStartTime.isAfter(...date.end...)) return true; })` rejects a slot inside one of multiple same-day override intervals as soon as it evaluates any other interval that does not contain it, so schedules with split availability lose valid booking slots.

P1 confidence=100 packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/slots.ts:141 — `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` calculates the end boundary from the start timestamp, so a booking that starts before a host's working-hours end and extends past it passes the availability check.

P2 confidence=75 packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/slots.ts:579 — `const userSchedule = userAvailability.find(({ user: { id: userId } }) => userId === slotUserId);` adds a linear host lookup for every candidate-slot/user pair after the existing per-pair selected-slots scan, making large round-robin schedules scale quadratically instead of using an ID-keyed schedule map.

apps/web/test/lib/getSchedule.test.ts:788 — P2, confidence 75, verbatim `timeZone: Timezones["+6:00"]`: the timezone-compatibility change has no DST-transition or date-boundary acceptance test, so an override whose organizer and invitee dates differ across a daylight-saving offset change ships without verification that its slots remain on the intended local date.

apps/web/test/lib/getSchedule.test.ts:758 — P2, confidence 75, verbatim `users: [{ ...TestData.users.example, id: 101, schedules: [TestData.schedules.IstWorkHoursWithDateOverride(plus2DateString)] }]`: the new per-user override propagation has no collective or dynamic-host acceptance test, so a multi-host event can publish a slot when one host's override excludes it without the change being caught before release.

packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/slots.ts:114 — P1 confidence 100: `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` is always false because it compares two distinct Dayjs objects, so an all-day date override is treated as a bounded override and `getSchedule` reports every slot on that date as available instead of preserving the override's no-availability semantics.

apps/web/test/lib/getSchedule.test.ts:56 — P1, confidence 100, verbatim `.every((actualSlotTime, index) => { return `${dateString}T${expectedSlots[index]}` === actualSlotTime; })`: the newly added different-timezone assertion passes when the scheduler returns an empty or truncated slot list because `every` only validates produced slots and never asserts the expected four slots exist, so this test reports timezone compatibility while a regression removes override availability.

goldens.comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime

Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))

adjudication_records.issue_text: P1 confidence=100 packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/slots.ts:106 — `dateOverrides.find((date) => { ... if (slotEndTime.isBefore(...date.start...) || ... || slotStartTime.isAfter(...date.end...)) return true; })` rejects a slot inside one of multiple same-day override intervals as soon as it evaluates any other interval that does not contain it, so schedules with split availability lose valid booking slots.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a bug in the logic. Looking at lines 103-124, the code uses `dateOverrides.find()` which returns the first matching element. Inside the callback, when a date override matches the same day (line 107-109), it sets `dateOverrideExist = true` and then checks if the slot is outside that specific override's bounds (lines 110-121). If the slot is outside ONE override's bounds, it returns `true` from find(), causing the function to return `false` (slot unavailable). However, with multiple same-day overrides (split availability like 9-12 and 2-5), a slot at 10am would be rejected when evaluating the 2-5pm override because it's 'before' that override's start time, even though it's valid within the 9-12 override. The logic should check if the slot is within ANY of the overrides, not reject it if it's outside ANY single override.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that line 579 adds a `.find()` call inside a loop that processes slots for each user. Looking at the diff, this is within a `.map()` over `availableTimeSlots` (line 571-591), and for each slot it iterates through `slot.userIds` (line 573) and calls `userAvailability.find()` for each user. This is indeed O(slots * users * userAvailability.length) when it could be O(slots * users) with a pre-built map. This is a legitimate performance concern for the new code, though it's an optimization issue rather than a bug - the code is functionally correct but has suboptimal algorithmic complexity for large datasets.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that on line 114, the code compares two distinct Dayjs objects using `===`, which will always return false because JavaScript compares object references, not values. The correct approach would be to use `.isSame()` method. This means the condition intended to detect all-day date overrides (where start equals end) will never trigger, causing incorrect behavior where all-day overrides are treated as bounded overrides.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/test/lib/getSchedule.test.ts:56 — P1, confidence 100, verbatim `.every((actualSlotTime, index) => { return `${dateString}T${expectedSlots[index]}` === actualSlotTime; })`: the newly added different-timezone assertion passes when the scheduler returns an empty or truncated slot list because `every` only validates produced slots and never asserts the expected four slots exist, so this test reports timezone compatibility while a regression removes override availability.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a test weakness. Looking at the diff, the test uses `toHaveTimeSlots` which likely uses `.every()` to check that returned slots match expected slots. If the scheduler returns an empty array `[]`, then `[].every(...)` returns `true`, meaning the test would pass even when no slots are returned. This is a real defect in the test logic - it doesn't verify that the expected number of slots (4) actually exist, only that whatever slots are returned match the expected pattern. This could mask a regression where timezone handling breaks and returns no slots.
